source.title: Statistical Mechanics and Artificial Neural Networks: Principles, Models, and Applications

record.file_problem: Text includes the full chapter and references; no truncation or garbling that prevents reading.
record.tranche_reason: The chapter presents a ResNet-56 trained on CIFAR-10 with training accuracy 100.00 and test accuracy 93.66, and argues against using flatness in random projections as a measure of generalization error. This bears on V7’s sharpness/generalization relationship, but it does not test magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.gate_note: The ResNet-56 training and test accuracy/loss are reported for context, not as a test of memorization capacity or a training-to-test error comparison across conditions. The chapter discusses cited sharpness work but supplies no direct magnitude-aware sharpness result.
record.test_reason: The chapter tests whether loss-landscape projections preserve saddle geometry, not whether magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance tracks generalization gaps. Even its filter-normalized random projections do not compare sharpness with gaps across networks. Its other results do not test V1–V6 or V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: random projections can misrepresent saddles as apparent minima, motivating caution about interpreting projected flatness as a generalization measure and favoring projections along dominant positive and negative Hessian directions. This conclusion does not establish a failure of V7's magnitude-aware sharpness correlation.
record.recipe_differences: The chapter studies loss-landscape geometry and projections, not magnitude-aware sharpness or the original generalization-measure comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: The interpretation of curvature changes with projection direction: random directions can suggest a local minimum where Hessian directions reveal a saddle.

fits_no_version.finding: Constructed saddle points appear non-saddle in about 30% of random projections in the balanced example and essentially all projections in the strongly imbalanced example (Sections 4.2.1–4.2.2, Figure 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Low-dimensional random loss projections can conceal saddle geometry; their apparent flatness does not reliably describe the original landscape.

fits_no_version.finding: ResNet-56 has Hessian eigenvalues −16.4 and 5007.9 at the examined solution. Hessian directions reveal a saddle, whereas filter-normalized random directions suggest a minimum (Section 4.3.1, Figure 11).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Filter-normalized random projections can conceal negative curvature in a trained image classifier.

fits_no_version.finding: For the 2- and 10-layer function approximators, searching Hessian-direction projections yields training losses over 9% and 26% lower and corresponding test losses about 1% and 6% lower than the random-projection comparisons (Section 4.3.2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dominant Hessian directions can expose nearby parameter settings with lower training and test loss than random-direction projections reveal.

record.problems: The cited ResNet-56 visualization is based on training loss; the chapter reports no test-set curvature or magnitude-aware perturbation comparison. The chapter's experiments on curvature use constructed loss functions and loss-landscape visualizations, not a direct test of the mapped generalization-gap claim.
record.rows_left_out: No result rows were kept. The ResNet-56 training and test losses and accuracies do not test a listed version; random-projection curvature results do not measure the magnitude-aware sharpness named in V7.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and chance-level held-out accuracy compared with natural-label generalization under the same training recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove the penalty.
Dropout effects on held-out error across data sizes and regularization settings.
The association between magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance and generalization gaps across comparably trained networks, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Test-accuracy effects of removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Change V7 from tested_not_extracted to not_tested. Reporting one ResNet's training and test accuracy supplies neither V1's random-label comparison nor V7's across-network sharpness–gap comparison. No result rows require repair, and no omitted result warrants a verdict on a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Memorizing random labels and generalizing on natural labels under standard training.
Width sweep past interpolation and resulting test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classification and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer held-out performance.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe changes.
Dropout effects on held-out error and interactions with augmentation or weight decay.

The reported ResNet-56 local curvature is not magnitude-aware sharpness, and the study does not relate perturbation tolerance to the training-test gap. It argues that random-projection flatness is not a reliable generalization measure.
Removing memorized examples and measuring test accuracy.
